items.prompt: Evaluate whether the highest-output option maximises profit using invented weekly output/revenue/total-cost options: 10 batches/N$1,000/N$800; 20/N$1,800/N$1,300; 30/N$2,400/N$2,000. All output sells and all relevant costs are included.
items.canonical_answer: The 30-batch option has more revenue, but profit is N$400. The 20-batch option earns N$500 against N$200 at 10 batches, so it maximises profit among the listed feasible choices. More output is beneficial only while the added revenue exceeds added cost; the table does not establish an unlisted global maximum.
marking_guidance: Argument for higher output (1): more revenue. Argument against (2): extra cost matters (1), N$400 below N$500 (1). Condition (1): supplied feasible choices and full costs. Judgement (2): choose 20 (1), greatest listed profit N$500 (1). Limitation (1): no unlisted choice assessed. Total 7.

items.prompt: Explain the error in claiming profit has been maximised merely because it rose from N$200 to N$400 while another feasible choice yields N$500.
items.canonical_answer: Profit has increased but is not the highest feasible profit. The N$500 alternative exceeds N$400, so the improvement does not establish maximisation.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): improvement mistaken for maximum. Boundary/test (1): compare with feasible N$500 alternative.

items.canonical_answer: The creation of goods and services to satisfy wants.
marking_guidance: Key term/meaning (1): creation of goods and services satisfying wants.

items.prompt: Identify one goods-producing activity and one service-producing activity using original examples.
items.canonical_answer: Making clay bowls produces goods; repairing bicycles provides a service.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): making a tangible good. Distinct characteristic/example (1): providing a service.

items.prompt: Explain how sustained stronger demand for bowls can increase the pottery’s demand for labour when extra workers are needed to produce additional saleable output.
items.canonical_answer: More orders create a reason to expand bowl output. Additional workers contribute to that output, so the firm’s derived demand for labour rises under the stated production condition. The final-product demand drives the factor demand.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): stronger bowl demand. Mechanism (2): more saleable output needed (1), workers contribute to expansion (1). Consequence (1): derived labour demand rises under stated condition.

items.prompt: Explain why buying another machine may increase demand for maintenance skills even if it replaces manual shaping tasks.
items.canonical_answer: The machine substitutes for shaping work but requires maintenance. Capital and maintenance labour are complements, so demand for that skill may rise despite reduced demand for another task.
marking_guidance: Context (1): different shaping and maintenance tasks. Reason/consequence (1): machine complements maintenance skill.

items.prompt: Explain the profit effect of replacing a labour-intensive method costing N$7,000 with a machine-assisted method costing N$6,200, each producing the same saleable quality and N$9,000 revenue; all relevant costs are included.
items.canonical_answer: The factor combination changes without changing revenue. Total cost falls N$800, raising profit from N$2,000 to N$2,800. The gain depends on the stated equal output, quality, sales and comprehensive cost conditions.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): factor substitution. Mechanism (2): cost falls N$800 (1), revenue unchanged (1). Consequence (1): profit rises N$800 with full costs included.

items.prompt: Explain why a wage saving alone is insufficient evidence that substituting a machine raises profit.
items.canonical_answer: Machine operation, maintenance, training and other relevant costs may offset the wage saving. Compare total costs and any revenue change before concluding profit rises.
marking_guidance: Context (1): wage saving is partial. Reason/conclusion (1): full costs and revenue determine net gain.

items.prompt: Define production (2). Identify two determinants of factor demand (2). Explain a reason to substitute capital for labour when the same saleable output can be produced at lower total relevant cost (2). Invented weekly choices with all output sold and all relevant costs included: 10 batches revenue N$1,000/cost N$800; 20 batches N$1,800/N$1,300; 30 batches N$2,400/N$2,000. Identify the profit-maximising output and its profit among the choices (2).
items.canonical_answer: Production creates goods and services to satisfy wants. Output demand and factor productivity influence factor demand. Lower total cost at unchanged revenue raises profit and can motivate capital substitution. Profits are N$200, N$500 and N$400; 20 batches gives the greatest listed profit of N$500.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): goods/services created (1), satisfy wants (1). Separate points (2): output demand (1), factor productivity (1). Explanation (2): cost reduction with same output (1), profit increase at unchanged revenue (1). Identification (2): 20 batches (1), N$500 (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented pottery methods for identical quality and 100 pieces sold weekly: labour-intensive total relevant cost N$7,000; machine-assisted total relevant cost N$6,200 including operation, maintenance and training. Each earns revenue N$9,000. The machine replaces some shaping tasks but requires skilled operation. Buyers demand the 100 pieces and required operators are available. No other feasible method is described. Describe production, the profit goal and the difference between revenue and profit using this case (6). Explain how product demand and factor substitution affect the choice and factor demand (7). Discuss whether the machine method can be called profit maximising (7).
items.canonical_answer: The pottery creates bowls satisfying wants. Profit maximisation seeks the greatest feasible revenue-cost difference; N$9,000 is revenue, with profits N$2,000 and N$2,800. Buyers support output and derived factor demand. Capital replaces shaping tasks, complements operation skills and lowers cost N$800 at unchanged revenue. The machine method is best of the two described, subject to quality, cost coverage and saleability. It cannot be established as the greatest of all feasible methods when alternatives are unspecified.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): production creates output (1), bowls satisfy wants (1); maximum profit goal (1), greatest feasible difference (1); revenue N$9,000 (1), profit after cost (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): buyers demand output (1), derived factor demand (1), substitution of shaping capital (1), complementary operators (1), total cost N$800 lower (1), revenue unchanged (1), profit N$800 higher (1). Both sides/judgement (7): machine N$2,800 (1), exceeds labour N$2,000 (1); required operators/quality condition (1), sales/full cost condition (1); other methods unassessed (1); judgement best listed (1), wider maximum not established (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented same-quality methods for a private pottery. Case 1: strong confirmed orders permit full utilisation; total weekly revenue N$9,000 under either method, full relevant cost N$7,000 labour-intensive or N$6,200 machine-assisted. Required machine skills and reliable power are available. Case 2: weak orders leave machinery idle; total weekly revenue is N$3,000 under either method and full relevant cost is N$2,500 labour-intensive or N$3,200 machine-assisted. The machine replaces some manual tasks in both cases; these are the two feasible methods. Evaluate capital substitution for profit maximisation in Case 1 (7). Evaluate it in Case 2 (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: substitution lowers full cost N$800, increasing profit from N$2,000 to N$2,800. The recommendation depends on confirmed sales, reliability, skills and equal quality, so machine assistance is best of the two. Case 2: idle machinery carries costs without corresponding sales; labour earns N$500 while machine assistance loses N$200. Retain the labour method under these demand conditions; stronger orders or different full costs could change the result.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for N$800 cost saving (1), profit N$2,800 (1); argument against reliance on sales (1), operational feasibility (1); condition confirmed demand/skills/power (1); judgement substitute (1), highest of feasible options (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument against idle capital cost (1), loss N$200 (1); argument for possible machine gain if demand changed (1), substitution can lower cost at utilisation (1); condition weak current orders (1); judgement labour (1), profit N$500 exceeds alternative (1). Total 14.
